chunks: "Quiescent current is the current a regulator draws from its input just to stay alive and regulate, with nothing on the output.
It's the bias current for the reference, the error amplifier, the feedback divider and the control logic.
On an LDO it flows out of the ground pin, so it's also called ground current, and it's just input current minus output current. It matters because it never goes away.
At a 1 amp load a 50 microamp Iq is irrelevant, but if my device sleeps at a few microamps, the regulator can be most of the sleep current.
A 220 milliamp-hour coin cell with a 52 microamp sleep current lasts about 176 days, but with 3 microamps it could last years, so Iq is what determines standby life.
It also kills light-load efficiency: at 10 microamps of load, a 50 microamp Iq means under 20 percent efficiency.

So for always-on rails I'd look for nanoamp-class Iq parts, and I'd check whether Iq changes with load or mode: some LDOs draw more ground current at heavy load, and switching regulators have a low Iq when idling but a much higher current while actually switching."
